utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. May we have the appearances for today, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Matthew Olmsted, and Crispian Smith, case manager, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic, Dragan Krgovic and Miroslav Cuskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could the Usher escort the witness back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Tutus, again I remind you that you are still on your oath. Yes, Mrs. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Tutus, just before we leave the parade, we can see painted on the vehicles, in fact, Judge Harhoff raised it, the words "Milicija." Just for the avoidance of any doubt, milicija was the name for the police, it was not? It doesn't mean military?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Next I want to move to the -- the "Glas" article that was -- at least I hope I am. I now need to say I haven't got it with me -- yes, I have. It was marked 1D032165 MFI. I don't think it was tendered yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am going to ask Your Honours, you remember I raised this, that -- it is, in fact, an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is an article in "Glas," and you were asked about it, of the 24th of April, and is this right: It -- it was the reaction to statements apparently made by Mr. Muharem Krzic, who was the president of the SDA in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we please read what you are referring to, because I don't really remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't catch the answer. Can we just go back for a moment to -- yes. Okay. If we go in the English to the second page, you were asked about statements you had made. I think it's all on the same page in the original. And in the article, about halfway through, the reporter quotes you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please read the quotation you're referring to? The letters are tiny, so I can't really read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. That's my fault, Mr. Tutus. This is what the reporter says that you said: "Mr. Muharem Krzic has for a long time been systematically attacking the CSB and the SJB of Banja Luka. My assessment says this is a deliberate construction aiming to break up the unity and efficiency of the service and so create a wartime atmosphere in the area." Can you see that? I think it may be marked, about -- on the right-hand column. If we go that way. Yes. Yes. Do you see it now?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now that you've read it, I remember that's how it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And what I want to ask you about is what the reporter says you said. "I shall just say, by way of illustration, that the declaration of loyalty to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina has so far been signed by 73 per cent of the Croats and 61 per cent of the Muslims of the previous number of people employed in our SJB." First, did you say that to the reporter?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And from where did you get the statistics?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were obtained for me by my -- at my request by the clerk. I asked -- named Momcilo Savic. I asked him for this information so that I would know how many people stayed. It refers not to the total number of employees of the Banja Luka Public Security Station but the total number of Croats and the total number of Muslims. So of that number, this is the percentage that stayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, are you able to tell us now what the total number of Muslims in the three security -- in the SJB plus the -- the police stations that came within its area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. What about Muslims? Are you able to tell us that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, no. You say 61 per cent of the Muslims had signed the oath of loyalty. How many Muslims were there altogether working in the SJB or the other police stations?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point in time I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And this was your response, was it, to criticisms that had been made by Mr. Krzic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a previous article, he put forward some incorrect information concerning the numbers of Muslims and Croats in the Banja Luka Public Security Station. He said there were only six. That was a lie, a fabrication. Before that, he had said untruths in public. For example, when there was an explosion near the mosque, and I remember that "Oslobodjenje" published him saying everyone knows except the chief. So it turned out that I had been informed of that event, and, in fact, I hadn't. So those were all lies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What, nobody had told you about an explosion at the mosque?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an explosion at a mosque. A hand-grenade had been thrown on it. And the Party of Democratic Action made a public statement, signed by Krzic, saying that they had informed me personally of this event. This was untrue. They had not informed me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So are you saying you did know about the explosion or you didn't know about the explosion?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about the explosion later on, but it wasn't true that the Party of Democratic Action informed me about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to move on to religious --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Korner, perhaps the witness remembers how many -- how many persons, how many Muslims stayed and how many Croats stayed. So the 73 per cent would represent how many persons, and the 60-whatever, 61 per cent would represent how many persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really don't know that. I don't know those numbers. These percentages are obtained for me by the service, but I don't know what the numbers were. I know that some did remain and were -- went on working in that period and are still there today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, that's all I want to ask you about this article.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, there have been a number of questions on it. I would ask now that it be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We object. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1095, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, next can we move, please, to the operative work plan and the various questions that you were asked about it. Now, you were only shown a part of these documents, I think, which was marked as 1D001267.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know what the exhibit number was, but, in fact, Your Honours, that document is part of a Prosecution document with the 65 ter number 2680, and I'd like, because it's all one document, this, and I'd like to look at it in that form. Oh, it's already an exhibit, is it? 860.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tutus, the first part of this document, which was all one document when it was received or put together, is a report dated the 17th of April, 1992, on what's called "Security Incidents Increase in Crime in the Area of Banja Luka SJB." And it contains a number of documents. It does not appear to be signed by anybody, if we look at the last page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could we have the P, please. I don't want the 1D exhibit, I want the P exhibit, which is P860. That's not P860. That's the Milos report. Yes, that's it. Can we look at the last page. I don't think there's any signature on it. The last page -- the last page of the document doesn't help, no. All right. Go back to the first page, please, because it's two documents. Sorry, can we go back to the first page in English?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Do you recognise, Mr. Tutus, this report? It appears to come, in fact, from the CSB rather than from you, but it's about the SJB report -- area.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to look at the entire document. It's very hard for me to say based on just one page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, what it's saying is that in the statistical period from the 1st of April to the 17th of April, 1992, there were 13 terrorist attacks on buildings in the Banja Luka area. From your --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. In all fairness to the witness, he should be shown the document, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah, certainly. I wanted -- didn't want to waste time, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll give you, Mr. Tutus, a copy -- oh, no, we won't, because I didn't bring the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is it possible to print this out so that the B/C/S -- so that the witness can have a look at it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Perhaps you could just continue reading on the screen, Mr. Tutus, while that's done. And let us know when you've read the first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we move the page down so Mr. Tutus can see it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we can go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Can we go to the next page, please, just so Mr. Tutus can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is consulting the document, reading it, may I make, I don't know, an observation? I don't -- I don't see how these -- this document is one document, because it consists of obviously two completely different documents. One document is this information which the witness is -- is reading right now, dated 17th of April, 1992; and the second document is operative plan of 25th of May, 1992. I don't -- I don't really understand. I mean, it would be very difficult even for Your Honours to deal with such documents. If two documents are combined into one exhibit, I really don't see how are we -- are we doing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, please remind me. Were they, in fact, exhibited as one, given one exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That is P860. Now, I have exhibited the other part during my cross-examination as -- as one document, which is definitely -- but I wonder how it happened that this document was -- I probably didn't notice at the time when it was -- when it was exhibited as 860, that it consists of two documents. I'm just suggesting that this -- this situation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- might be creating a problem in the future. That is all what I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- perhaps the -- in order to keep the sequence of numbering that we have, the Registry night --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. If Mr. Zecevic and Your Honours wait, there is purpose to why I'm dealing with this in this way, because as you will see there are some oddities about this whole document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I was only going to suggest that we preserve the number and just split it into A and B.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, we're saying that this is how the document came to us. And we're saying if you look at it, there are some oddities about the whole sequence, and Mr. Zecevic waits and Your Honours wait, you will see from my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will wait. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, have you had a chance to read that document, Mr. Tutus, now?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that a document that was prepared by your -- presumably your crime police?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was prepared by the crime police that was under our control, that is, in the public security station. Can you go back to page 1? I think it's a document issued by the security services centre, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is. It is. No, it's issued by the CSB, but would the information contained therein have come from your crime police in the SJB, or would it have been done by the crime section of the CSB?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably some initial operative information was sent by the crime prevention service to the centre, and I would not deny the fact that that information might be included in this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And one of the people this document refers to is Mr. Cavic, who we discussed when we looked at the report of the paramilitaries, you'll recall. You have to say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, it contains a list of attacks carried out with explosives devices between the 1st of April and the 17th of April, 1992, and there's a handwritten -- now let's move, please, to the document which is supposedly dated the 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In English, six pages in. And I imagine it's probably roughly the same in B/C/S. Page 7, thank you, in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is the one about which you were asked a great number of questions, I think, by both counsel for both accused. It begins -- and this is the operational work plan on solving acts of robbery, terrorism, et cetera, and it says: "From the 2nd to the 3rd of April, 1992, to this day, the 25th of May," and it talks about the SOS and then THE -- and then it says: "From the middle of August to this day, there have been 76 incidents of explosives devices ..." Now, it was put to you this is August 1991, but that's not what it says, is it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, it doesn't say so. I don't see the year.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. And why would this report in May 1992, when the earlier, 17th of April, talked about explosions, go back to August 1991?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite frankly, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well let's move further into this document, shall we? On page 2 in English, it deals with the incidents of explosions in the area of Banja Luka SJB.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I hope it's on page 2. The next page in English, and I hope the next page in B/C/S as well. And it's the paragraph near the end of the page in English. Okay. It would be the next page in B/C/S, it looks like. Yes. That's it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. If you allow me. The previous question you asked, I can try to think professionally why they go back to 1991. I can suppose that the service had certain statistics about crimes for that period as well, back to 1991, then they received information later about perpetrators and included the prior period as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The -- the list that went with it doesn't refer to anything in 1991. It refers to incidents in 1992, doesn't it? You went through that with either Mr. Zecevic or Mr. Krgovic yesterday.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, let's just have a look at this paragraph then. "In order to solve the incidents of explosion in the area of Banja Luka SJB, work on solving a series of explosions which according to intelligence were set off by a group of people headed by Vedran Mandic. Information indicates that this group committed 27 crimes of causing public danger by setting off explosive devices, hand-grenades and firing rockets at buildings. "The group consists of Draza Burnic; Drasko Mihajlovic, deceased; Mr. Maric; and Nenad Kajkut, deceased." Now, those are the two people who together with Mr. Mandic launched the attack on or killed -- not launched the attack, were killed in the course of an incident Mejdan police station; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's true, the police station Mejdan.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. About which no report was put in, as we saw yesterday, until June, I believe it is. June the 30th. Because you were directed to a criticism by -- apparently written by Mr. Zupljanin that it had taken so long to report. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That incident and the on-site investigation and the investigation was within the jurisdiction of the CSB, and the public security station was not involved. The on-site investigation was carried out the very next day. The investigating judge was present and all this was under the supervision of the CSB.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And interestingly enough, Vedran Mandic was also killed in that attack, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then, why doesn't it say, "Vedran Mandic, deceased"?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You see, what I'm wondering is that -- is that date actually correct of the 25th of May on this so-called operative work plan? Are you able to assist?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean that incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it happened?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no. The -- this report, this operational work plan about which you've been asked so much which allegedly is the 25th of May. Can you help us whether that date is actually right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next I want to move to the question of religious destruction in Banja Luka, in the Banja Luka area. You were asked to look at document 1D01130 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Before you move on, Ms. Korner, to the extent that the witness, as I understand his evidence, has not assisted in clearing up this curiosity, for want of a better word, about the date, does that still not leave us with the possible confusion to which Mr. Zecevic referred? And I come back to my suggestion about separating the number between an A and a B so when we come to look at this, we don't confuse ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we can't say one way or another where the -- how accurate all of this is. What we can say is that when we received the document or the documents, they were one document. That's how we got it, and that's why it's together and it was translated together, and it bears the ERN numbers together. Just a moment, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic has decided to separate them up and put that in as a separate exhibit. I'm not sure that that is the right way of looking at it. And therefore, we suggest that -- there's already a separate copy, but this is the way the document was, and we suggest it should stay together. We may get some elucidation later about whether it is actually produced at the time which it is said and represents something that actually happened. So that's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, Mrs. Korner, if your point is that the two documents were actually conceived at the same time, either in April or May --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Or later. Your Honours, we're suggesting later because we're not sure the reference to August is actually a reference to August 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: In any case, for the Chamber to make an assessment of whether there's anything to it, we need to be shown the reasons why you think that they may be conceived simultaneously. And thus, my question is: If your suspicion hangs only on the facts that Vedran Mandic was not indicated as deceased, as were the two other gentlemen who were killed apparently at the same date, then I am not sure that I am convinced by your argument that there is any possibility that these should -- two documents should be drafted together at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's not just that. The report on the death of the three men at the Mejdan police station, as Your Honours saw yesterday, was not actually sent until the 30th of June. Our possible suggestion, and I can put it no higher than that, Your Honour, and all we're dealing with at the moment is whether this exhibit should stay as one exhibit or two exhibits, because it is already an exhibit in the case, is that if you look at that plus the reference to August, it may well be that those documents were drafted at a later date, and that's the only suggestion which, on the face of what's there, we're entitled to make at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I fully understand your -- that road down which you're headed. My only question is: Inasmuch as this is a matter for argument and there will be -- of some controversy, what level it will reach it remains to be seen, whether to the extent that it appears on the face of it to be from the dates, two documents, whether we should not, for ease of reference, just so identify them. I don't see how it would harm your -- the case that you will put at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I'm perfectly happy if it -- if it makes Your Honours happier, that we mark it A and B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, you want to be heard on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did not mean to object at this stage of Mrs. Korner's examination, but I do have to object now. Mrs. Korner is misleading the witness and misrepresenting the document, creating a confusion which really doesn't exist concerning the status of Vedran Mandic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel is now too far away from the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document speaks about a group led by -- that was led by Vedran Mandic. In all the other passages we see references such as "led by," and this one is the only exception. The group was led by Vedran Mandic. So there is really no confusion. At the moment of the creation of this document, it is clear that he no longer leads that group, that he was its leader, and then follow indications who is dead and who is alive. Look at the name Palackovic. It says "is leading the group." Vedran Mandic is the only one who finds himself in the past tense. So there is really no doubt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We will mark the document A and B and move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have a look at 1D208 about which you were asked during cross-examination. Now, this is the -- the note from Mr. Bulic, the head of the crime police, I think, number 2 to Zupljanin in the CSB, talking about: "The Banja Luka Bishop's Ordinate has informed us there had been fire at the convent building and parish church in Bosanski Aleksandrovac. Since attacks of religious buildings are also occurring in other places in the area, it is necessary to take steps in order to stop such events and identify the perpetrators of the act reported so far." And you were asked about this at page 7823 on Friday, and you said you didn't remember the attack on the church and the convent building in Bosanski Aleksandrovac. Is that right, you don't remember that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. Bosanski Aleksandrovac is in the area of another public security station, not Banja Luka, but either Laktasi or Gradiska. It's not in the Banja Luka SJB area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I know, but surely somebody firing on a Catholic convent building and a parish church was worthy of note in Banja Luka. You don't remember anything about it at all?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were such incidents. There were more serious incidents. One pushed out the other from our focus. There were many such events. At the time I was informed, but I no longer remember everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. That's right, wasn't it? Although the major explosions of -- as against mosques in Banja Luka happened in 1993, that is to say, the Ferhadija mosque, and I think the Arnaudija mosque; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to object. How is this -- what is the reason for this question? It's outside the period of the indictment, and the question goes beyond the scope of cross-examination. It concerns an explosion from 1991. I don't remember anyone asking any questions about this event from 1993 in cross-examination, plus it's outside the period of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I haven't even finished the question before the objection. The -- first of all, it's nothing to do with 1991. This document is dated July 1992, and I was setting the scene for the question, which I was in the middle of, and I will repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Although the major destruction took place in 1993, in 1992, Mr. Tutus, there were a number, weren't there, of serious attacks against religious institutions in the Banja Luka area?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, this says you must take steps in order to stop such events, and your response when you were asked about this, the question was at page 7823: "As part of your responsibilities in the Banja Luka SJB, did you take any steps and measures in order to prevent religious facilities, religious buildings from being attacked, and did you take measures to identify perpetrators of crimes that had been reported at the time?" Your response: "We certainly acted in accordance with this letter, and at meetings we conveyed the order issued." Now, I'm going to ask the same question that you were asked, I think, by Mr. Zecevic. Did you take any steps and measures in order to prevent religious facilities or religious buildings from being attacked?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our specific task was to use police patrols to tour these buildings more frequently. I remember issuing an order that every police station in its own area should pay special attention to religious buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Most of these attacks on the religious buildings, which in 1992 included, did it not, the -- sorry, let me just get my -- the Pecinska mosque?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the names.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The Petricevac Franciscan monastery? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that convent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The premises of the Islamic Community, which is close to the Ferhadija mosque?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In that case those explosive devices were thrown, as I said. I believe a hand-grenade was thrown on that mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And is it right that most of these attacks took place at night?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you place police officers or reserve police officers of whom you had a number, as we've discussed, on guard at these places to prevent these attacks?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how the station commander assigned the staff and how he gave them specific tasks, but he had received an order from me to pay special attention and give special protection to religious buildings. Whether they assured constant presence and security details, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's go to the next topic you were asked about, please. You were shown the document P367, I think it is, the record of the meeting of the 6th of May at the CSB.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we need to move to the page, which I think is probably the fourth page in English, where Mr. Zupljanin says: "In all our activities we are obliged to abide by." Thank you very much. And I think it's probably in the second page in the B/C/S. Paragraph 23. Yes. Thank you very much. If you can just highlight a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, it was suggested to you that that referred only to disarmament. Now, obviously you can't say what was in the mind of Mr. Zupljanin when he made this statement, but is it your evidence that the words "in all our activities we are obliged to observe all measures and apply all procedures ordered by the Crisis Staff of the autonomous region," applied only to disarmament?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it concerns only disarmament.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Next, you were asked about Simo Drljaca, and you described how Mr. Zupljanin had said he would -- I'm paraphrasing, he would pay for what he had done in Prijedor, and it was suggested to you that that was said as a -- during or as a result of the 11th of July meeting. Now, in meetings that you attended at the CSB in -- towards the end of August and later, was there discussion of the killings that had taken place at Koricanske Stijene, Vlasic Mountain, by the Prijedor police?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no discussion of that at the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was it ever discussed at all at any of the meetings which the SJB chiefs attended at the CSB in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't mean it the way you said. Chiefs of the CSB, that may mean the senior collegium --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I mean chiefs --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but I don't remember it was discussed at the professional council meetings that I attended.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So you don't recall any discussion at meetings you attended, which is where the SJB chiefs were, of what had happened at Mount Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But weren't the SJB in Banja Luka crime police assigned to investigate the case?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So can you now recall in what context Zupljanin make that remark to Simo Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told you. He criticised Simo and told him he would be held responsible for what had happened in Prijedor, but he didn't say precisely what he meant by that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And now finally, can we move to the question of the SOS and the Special Police about which you were asked a lot of questions. It was put to you at one stage that you couldn't say that all the members of the SOS were criminals. Do you remember that being put to you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that something like that was asked of me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And do you know, one way or another, whether all of the SOS were criminals?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that. I know what I was told by my colleagues. They told me that there were individuals who were well-known criminals and who had criminal records.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like you to have a look, please, at the report that you did put in to the public -- or what was put in by the CSB to the public prosecutor's office on those three men who were killed at Mejdan police station. I'm afraid I've forgotten what the exhibit number is but it's 1D010230. 1D57. 2D57. And this is the one where you say you recognised -- do you recognise the writing or is it just Zupljanin's initials?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the handwriting is his.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And he says he wants to know why you've had to wait so long. Now, it says on the 30th of June, 1992, you received our report. Vedran Mandic; Nenad Kajkut, son of Nikola; and then Drasko Mihajlovic. This is, is it not, a different Kajkut to Nenad Kajkut, although the name's the same, to the gentleman who's in the Special Police. Obviously, as we'll see, because that person is still alive and kicking, but do you know?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of only one Nenad Kajkut.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, in that case he did a remarkable return from the grave, but anyhow. What I want to ask you about is this: If you look, please -- now -- yes, okay. In English it's the ninth page in English. And in the B/C/S it is the fourth page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. No. No. Whatever that is, I don't know. In English, starting with that it's one, two -- that's it. Top paragraph. And in B/C/S, as I say, it should be -- sorry, it's the eighth page in B/C/S. Yes. Sorry. Eighth page. My fault.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is where -- this is where the -- the witness whose statement this is, and I think you looked at part of it, it's the -- it's the Official Note - sorry - provided by Mr. Petar Tanazovic, and you were asked about this, is recording what Mr. Vedran Mandic is saying to him. "He told me that he was a member of the SOS and that he was at the barricades when it was necessary to be there because that was what the politicians demanded, but now when they did not need us, nobody was taking care of us. I told him that he was wrong and that he had the opportunity to report to the district TO staff, just as the rest of his comrades had done. However, he brushed this aside, saying he did not trust anyone and that he acted only on Nenad Stevandic's orders ..." Now, do you know whether at any stage any investigation was carried out by the SJB, you, or the CSB into Nenad Stevandic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not within the competence of the Banja Luka Public Security Station. As to whether the centre or the National Public Security Service did something about this, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The witness says whether the national state security or CSB Banja Luka did anything, he is not aware, and it wasn't recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And is that because, to your knowledge, Mr. Stevandic was a part of, you said the state security service, which I think was still in those days the SDB as opposed to the SNB. Was that because you were aware Mr. Stevandic was a part of that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that he was a part of that service, and that's not the reason, but the reason is it was not within our competence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But then why did you mention, as Mr. Zecevic had just said, why did you mention the state security if you didn't know Mr. Stevandic had anything to do with it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned the National Security Service because I felt that armed rebellion fell within their purview. They were tasked with gathering information on such things.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But are you saying this incident was armed rebellion?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how else to describe it. If a group of 20 -- 200 armed men suddenly turns up in the streets.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see. You're back to -- all right. You're back to the SOS. I was talking about this incident here at Mejdan police station. All right. Finally, last topic, thank you, Mr. Tutus, back to the Special Police. Now, you were asked a number of -- you were shown Mr. Dubocanin's card which appears to show that he was a member of the military, and then you were asked a number of questions about the list of the Special Police and also the payroll for August. And it was suggested to you that these people, under some agreed deal, although they were not members of the police, had received payment in August. Now, I want you to look, please, at a document which relates to three of the people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's dated -- sorry, I can't just find it. Yes. Now, Your Honours, this one, although it was on my original list, we noted that it had not -- it was not on our 65 ter list, and it's part of the application we made in February, February the 18th, to add. The document number bears -- the old number is 65 ter 275 and it appears in schedule E, and we haven't had a response to it but I'm going to ask whether I can use it subject to your response. It was on my original list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I vigorously object to that because we had the ruling about the using documents which is not in the 65 ter list, so I vigorously object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- I assume, Mrs. Korner, that your application is to merely use it at this point, not admit it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Exactly. I'll use it and have it marked for identification subject to Your Honours' ruling. I mean, can I say we've given enough notice that we wanted to use it. It's February the 18th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you have a look, please, at 65 ter 275. Oh, we need, sorry, page 2 in English and page 2 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is dated the 31st of December, 1992. It's addressed to the chief of the National Security Service sector and then to the police brigade command. Firstly, by the end of 1992, had a police brigade been set up?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 31st of December, is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. By the 31st of December, 1992, had a police -- an actual police brigade been set up?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what follows from this order. The command was being set up as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I'm asking whether you were aware of it as a police officer in Banja Luka, please. Not what this order says. We can all read that.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you're asking me, I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, the order is: "In order to improve the quality of execution of combat tasks in the Banja Luka CSB Police Brigade, I hereby appoint: "Ljuban Ecim, as commander of the 1st Battalion; Zdravko Samardzija, assistant battalion commander; and Nenad Kajkut, commander of the 1st Company of the 1st Battalion. And then the chief of the national security sector must appoint an assistant." Now, would Mr. Zupljanin have been able to appoint people --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection. First, the Prosecutor should ask the witness whose signature this and whether the document was signed by Stojan Zupljanin, and then she could put this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think it is. I think it's signed on his behalf by Mr. Bulic, but if you want to take that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just tell us?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you able to say who signed this document on -- over Mr. Zupljanin's typed signature?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was signed by Djuro Bulic, the chief of the public security sector, the CSB in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does it say "za" somewhere, "on behalf of"?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, if there's any point -- any further point that needs to be taken on that. What I want to know is: Whether it was signed by Mr. Bulic on behalf of Mr. Zupljanin or not, would it appear that these three men, including, I would suggest, a different Mr. Kajkut from the one that was killed at Mejdan, were appointed by Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say they were appointed by the security services centre. As to what the result of their agreements and talks was, I wouldn't be able to say with any precision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, may I have that marked for identification pending Your Honours' ruling?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1096, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then finally, let's just have one last look, please, at the payroll for August document and the attached list of Special Police. Again I've forgotten the exhibit number. I've got 65 ter 23 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise. Just to clarify a point linked to this document. Is it the position of the Prosecution that this document has something to do with the Special Police, the document shown previously, because if that is the OTP position, then this document is being misinterpreted. It does not refer to the Special Police or any special unit of the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is [indiscernible]. This is argument. We are saying three members, and I'm just going to confirm, of the ex-Banja Luka Special Police, including the two leaders, are still under the command of Zupljanin by the end of 1992. That's what we're saying. Still connected with the CSB. The suggestion was made at length and rather boringly, for which, quite honestly [indiscernible] Mr. Krgovic did it, that none of these people stayed in the police. That is not the case, we say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, as you say, Ms. Korner, all of this is a matter for argument. What I thought Mr. Krgovic's objection was going to be - and I know when you were putting the question, this is immediately before the document was marked for identification - that Mr. Krgovic had begun to rise and apparently had a change of mind. And I, too, was wondering - I don't know whether the objection that he was considering making was what was running through my own mind - that the document not being exhibited, merely being shown to the witness, you were asking the witness to comment on this -- on this, on the accuracy of the contents of this document which you would have known at that point would not have been exhibited at this point. But then the witness's answer of not being able to assist, to my mind, made that -- that any such objection of no consequence, and for that same reason the -- as you say, at this point everything is a matter of argument, so we move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you have one last look, please, at Exhibit P1092. Number 4 on the payroll is Nenad Kajkut. Do you agree? And it's signed for.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So clearly there are two gentlemen pottering around Banja Luka at this time called Nenad Kajkut, unless he didn't die in Mejdan. You were taken through a number of people on the list of Special Police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which we need to go, please, to the one, two, three, fourth page in English and pretty much the same, I hope, in B/C/S. Actually, I think it's the fifth page in B/C/S. Sorry, it's the seventh page in B/C/S and the -- oh, no, sorry, not the fourth page in English. Eighth. It's eighth page in both. This appears, does it not -- I think we've been through this before and you've been asked, but this is a list of the Special Police detachment as it was before it was abolished and effectively what happened to them since the abolition. Is this -- is that right? Where they went to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection. This is a leading question, because from this document the movement of members of this detachment after it was disbanded cannot be seen, because there are notes on their movements while the unit or the detachment was actually in existence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know on what possible basis you can say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Let's move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Can I just -- can I just say, Mr. Krgovic, not helping matters. You went through this document at length for your purposes. I now propose to try and correct the impression you made.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, if we look, please, at number 11, Mr. Vojislav Burgic, he apparently is at the SJB in Laktasi as a reserve policeman. Number 14, Mr. Borjan, SJB Novi Grad, active policeman; Mr. Zarko Bulaja, SJB, active policeman; Mr. Predrag Bodiroza, SJB Banja Luka, training course graduate; Mr. Blagojevic, CSB Banja Luka, active policeman. You went -- were taken through this. Does it appear that numbers of the special unit remained in some form or other in the police service, some indeed in the CSB Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you -- you were asked to look at a number of criminal complaints that were brought against, in particular, members of the SOS, and you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor when you were interviewed numbers of documents relating to the Special Police and also prosecutions. Now, first, are you able to recall whether there were any criminal prosecutions in respect of the various members of the Special Police that you named in your various reports?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there were criminal prosecutions, prosecutions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And where are, please, the documents that relate to those prosecutions?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They should be in the court and in the operative records of the crime prevention police of the present security service.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. When you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor interviewer in 2004 copies of various documents, where did you get those documents from? You declined to tell the Office of the Prosecutor then, but I'm asking you now.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. What do you mean by declining to tell something?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You turned up with a whole pile of documents which you handed over to the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you remember that in your interview? Mr. Sebire, the investigator, was asking you questions, took copies.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I remember that. And I wish to tell Their Honours that I was at that time suspected of being a member of a joint criminal enterprise. I was told of my rights, and I was offered the opportunity to have a defence counsel present. I did not feel I needed to have counsel. I agreed to be interviewed. I had certain documents with me which I used for my defence. During the break, there was a lady there from the OTP, and there was this gentleman. I think his name was Nicholas. And they looked at the documents to see where I was getting my information from, and they asked me to give them those documents, which I did, and that is correct. Yes, all of that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely. You're quite right, Mr. Tutus. And it's a simple question. Where did you get the documents from that you gave to Mr. Sebire?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I happened to have those documents there because I was still -- when I was still the chief of the station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right, but where in the station did you get those documents from?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't find them in the station. When I received the summons for the suspect interview, I prepared for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I quite understand, Mr. Tutus. You're going around the houses now. Just tell us where you got those documents from that you gave to the investigator.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had them. They were in my possession.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sure you did. And how did you get them?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, ask me about a particular document and I'll tell you. Most of them were given to me by Zoran Jusic, the chief of the crime police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. That's all I'm asking. And is he still at the SJB in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you very much, Mr. Tutus. That's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I may follow up on Mrs. Korner's last question. This bundle of documents that you received, did you exercise -- did you decide what to select, or you just received these and handed them over to the investigator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the most important piece of information from 1993, which we compiled at the request of Tomo Kovac, the chief of the public security sector, it contained all the information I had with me, and there was no reason to deny the OTP that. And there was a dispatch concerning the attack at Tunjice and a criminal complaint where we took into custody a member of the Special Police detachment and that was it. But I didn't make an overview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry. The question that I really wish to ask, Mr. Tutus, is what, if anything, are we to make of the fact that apparently this bundle of documents didn't include any records of prosecutions of persons in respect of whom complaints -- either you made complaints or you're aware that complaints were made. What -- is there anything that we should make of that absence or gap?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not deal with the archives. I didn't feel I needed to have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when this witness started to answer, there was a small imprecision in the interpretation which led to confusion, so if you'll allow me to clarify this point during the cross-examination, because the witness said something that was not interpreted correctly and throws a different interpretation on the whole matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tutus, when you were answering the question there was some confusion. When you answered the question as to how you came into possession of that document, you said: "Those documents happened to be in my office while I was still chief of the Banja Luka Public Security Station." That's what you said, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And when Mrs. Korner asked me who gave them to me, I told them the chief of the crime prevention department, Josic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And he gave them to you at the time that these documents were actually compiled?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So in 1993, not after you left the public security station?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. In that period, because they were characteristic and I felt I needed to have them with me because I felt they were important for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Josic is now a lawyer in Banja Luka and has nothing to do with the public security station; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that's how I understood this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm very grateful to Mr. Krgovic because there was a misunderstanding. I had understood that Mr. Josic had given them to him for the purposes of the interview. Your Honours, may I just go back over this for a minute then.

utterances.speaker: MRS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why did you keep -- when you left Banja Luka S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I had -- I had not ignored but I had gone past the break thinking we would finish this witness. And we've reached the point now, at 10.32, whether, in fact, we shouldn't take the break and just complete this witness when we come back.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's all I -- I mean, this is the only point that I still want to get cleared up, but if Your Honours have more questions then it would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MRS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Tutus, just a -- it's a really simple point this, now that we've cleared up the misunderstanding thanks to Mr. Krgovic. When you left the SJB Banja Luka, you took with you, did you, copies of a number of documents from the period you'd been there?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't do it for any particular purpose, but as events unfolded, the crime police brought me copies of documents that were typical in their opinions for my information, for the purpose of informing other prosecution organs. There was one, for instance, typical criminal report concerning the murder of Milan Kocic. Sometimes I brought them home and left them there. All the copies of various articles from the "Glas" newspaper I also kept.

utterances.speaker: MRS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't quite understand. Is it because the crime police and you felt that things were not being done as they ought that they were giving you copies of these various documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: MRS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I want to know what you mean by: "The crime police brought me copies of documents that were typical in their opinions for my information."

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for example, let me give you the example of one document. A copy of a criminal report against one group of former members of the Special Police detachment who kidnapped Milan Kocic near the Internacional Hotel. They killed him, threw the car in the river, and then when their houses were searched, a certain amount of weapons was found. The crime police did all the work. These perpetrators were detained, and they brought me this file as an example of how they -- how successfully they had dealt with this job.

utterances.speaker: MRS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So can we take this -- because I don't want to spend so much time on this. You provided to the -- the investigator during the course of your interview documents 2506, 2507, 8, 9, 10, all matters connected with the Special Police. So you had kept or been given copies of matters which related to the Special Police. Why was that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you precisely why, because it was in the jurisdiction of the CSB. Some of it remained in my possession and some of it in the possession of the CSB. I don't have all of it, but all of it is certainly in the CSB.

utterances.speaker: MRS. KORNER
utterances.text: But why were you concentrating, certainly as far as the interview was concerned, so heavily on the documents that you had somehow acquired that related to the behaviour of the Special Police?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the conduct of some members of the Special Police to be problematic, and perhaps for that reason I kept some of those documents so that I can substantiate my arguments to that effect at the professional council meetings.

utterances.speaker: MRS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, I'm really sorry but I need to go back, if I may, with your permission, to this question of the 25th of May document, because in the break something has been drawn to my attention I think which puts this in the light which may make it clearer. May I have that permission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, before you do that, there was something I was going to say for the record when this witness had completed his testimony, and that is, having been so advised by the Registry, the proposal of separating this number between an A and B is technically not workable, so we're left with the original number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, can I -- Your Honours, can I ask, please, because I think this will deal with it, that the document which is 2D57 be put back on the screen, and can we go in both B/C/S to page 14 and in English to page 14.

utterances.speaker: MRS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is part of the file on the killing of the three men, Mr. Kajkut, Mr. Mandic, and Mr. Mihajlovic, that we've looked at quite often. And this is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have it in English, please. All right.

utterances.speaker: MRS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is to the public prosecutor's office, dated the 22nd of September, 1992. And I don't know why they're bothering when there are three dead men, but certainly it seems to be taken further. Can we look --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we don't have the Serbian --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that not it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It should be page -- you're quite right. 22nd of the 9th, 1992? Is that not the thing to the public prosecutor's office? No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm terribly sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page in each, please -- oh, no, stay on that page in B/C/S. No, sorry, sorry, go back. It's the page I want in B/C/S. Sorry. And could we go to the next page in English. And it's the second paragraph in English about these three men.

utterances.speaker: MRS. KORNER
utterances.text: "They committed these crimes between the 3rd of April, 1992, and the 16th of June, 1992, when they were killed during an armed attack on the Mejdan police station." And indeed I think you told us originally it was June that the attack took place. Is that right, Mr. Tutus?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact time. I really don't know the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MRS. KORNER
utterances.text: But the point that I want to make, and I don't want to have that document up again on the screen, is that report, allegedly dated the 25th of May, refers to these two men being -- two out of the three being deceased. Now, that is not possible, is it, because they weren't killed until the 16th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who said that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I mean, it's obviously misleading. Not leading, misleading completely, Your Honour. If you look at the rest of this document, you will see when this -- 6th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have here this document in front of me, but if you go further to this document, you find the exact date of this and when these men was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I know that's -- I had originally worked on the 6th of May and then I realised that's not right apparently. But anyhow, I don't think we can take this matter any further at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, with all due respect, it might be a typo. It might be a typo in this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Anything might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I agree with you but I'm just suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, that's why -- can I say it's now a matter for argument and comment and we'll see where we get to, but that's in effect what this report says. And, Your Honours, thank you very much. That's all I do ask this witness. Further Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tutus, I just have a small question for you in relation to something you told us yesterday in response to a question put to you by Mr. Krgovic. And if anyone wants to follow your testimony yesterday, it was yesterday's testimony at page 54, if you want to click back to the place. And let me read out to you what was entered into the transcript. Mr. Krgovic is saying the following to you: "I see that both you and the centre, the security services centre, filed a large number of criminal reports containing qualifications of these criminal offences, and I see that you are using the qualifications from the Criminal Code, murder, robbery, and you qualify them as regular crimes; is that right?" And your answer was: "Yes." And then Mr. Krgovic then goes on to say: "When my learned friend Mr. Zecevic and the Prosecutor were putting questions to you concerning dispatches concerning war crimes, you thought that as Banja Luka was not in the war theatre, you described these crimes the same way you would as in peacetime; is that correct?" And your answer was: "Yes." Mr. Krgovic then went on to say: "Regardless of the fact that persons of other ethnicities were the victims of the crimes, this did not, in your view, make it a war crime; is that correct?" And your answer is then that: "Well, we thought we should do the job in the way we did, but that doesn't mean that the prosecutor could not have altered that. As we were not actually in the war theatre, on the battle-field, we thought that this was the proper way to go about it." That's the testimony of yesterday. My question to you now is this: Would it have made any difference if you, as the police, had classified these documents right from the beginning as war crimes?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have made no difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So your testimony is that the procedure you would follow and the authority to which you would submit your reports would be the same regardless of whether it was a peacetime crime or a war crime; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let me just clarify one question with you, then. If in wartime a crime that could be characterised as a war crime was committed by a member of the armed forces, to whom would you report or what would the procedure be that would have to be followed in case of a war crime being committed in wartime? Would the police be involved at all, or would it be the military police who would assume the responsibility to investigate the crime?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: All this would have been done by the military justice and the military prosecutor, or perhaps they would have only asked us for assistance in terms of resources and technical assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And if you were then investigating a crime starting out from the assumption that this was a peacetime crime but reaching the conclusion that because of the nature of the crime and the circumstances under which the crime was committed you would end up finding that this could and should be treated as a war crime, would you then have submitted your report to the military police or to the military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if military organs were involved in the crime, then we would defer the case to the military security organs; and if we reached such conclusions in the course of the investigation, we would submit it to the military prosecutor. We would have done the same, basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't want Your Honours or the witness to mislead himself. He actually gave us a document which I didn't trouble to use but which is on this point. Can I ask that be it put up on the screen? It's 65 ter 2393. This is a document that he gave to us in interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Tutus, these are instructions on the implementation of the Law on Internal Affairs; is that right? Going back to 1986?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And which you -- do you remember giving those to the investigator?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look then, please, at the third page -- fourth -- third page in English, and in B/C/S also it's the third page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does that show in paragraph 5: "The centres act on crimes for which the penalty provided by law is a prison sentence in excess of ten years ..." And then halfway through that paragraph: "Crimes against humanity and international law."

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR TUTUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was Your Honour's question, so I just thought you better have a look at this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I understand that Ms. Korner was trying to assist the Trial Chamber on that, although I don't -- I don't know how it fits with the -- with the procedural rules, but in any case, I don't think, Your Honours, that it was exactly your question. Your question was quite different than this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: My question sprang out of the question that was left with me when the witness had offered his testimony yesterday, because I thought that it was somehow strange that these crimes would be characterised only as civil crimes while the whole thing was going on in -- at a time which was clearly wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand that quite clearly, but what I'm trying to say is that this document does not correspond or it does not assist the Trial Chamber in that respect with what your question was. I mean, we will, of course, explain during the course of the trial the nature of this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tutus, we thank you for your assistance to the Tribunal over the past several days. Your testimony's now at an end. You're released as a witness, and we wish you a safe journey back to your home. The Usher would now escort you from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mrs. Korner, you're on your feet. I don't know whether it is to articulate what you alluded to yesterday, that you would be making an oral application to -- yes. Could we hear you, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, can I -- the oral application that I'm going to make can be made in open session. The oral application that Mr. Olmsted will make on behalf of the next witness will have to be done in private. Your Honours, yesterday you delivered a ruling in private session because part of it related to timings for the trial, but this part, I take it, I can refer to in open session because it was an order to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, the order read that if for one or more of the 92 ter witnesses, more time in chief is needed than 20 minutes, in parenthesis because it doesn't occur on the transcript there, specifically to present new evidence for that part viva voce, as it were, the Trial Chamber expects the OTP to file a written motion with the reasons why, and it reads "how many extra time should be allotted," but I think that should be "how much extra time should be allotted." Your Honours then later said that because of the fact that two witnesses were due very shortly, we could deal with this orally. Your Honour, the witness who will come after the next witness, Mr. Mandic, Your Honours will know until Your Honours decided that it would be 20 minutes, we had put down six hours for, despite the fact that he's 11 days of transcript in the Krajisnik trial, a part of the 92 ter package. Accepting, therefore, that Your Honours will have read the 11 days of transcript, it is not proposed to go over with him what he said in that transcript. However, the trial of Krajisnik was not specifically geared towards the police. It was geared towards a member of the Presidency. We have therefore -- you will have seen, Your Honours, we provided a list of some 120 documents which we thought we might have to deal with through him. In actual fact, having gone -- may I say Mr. Mandic is at present, because he saw the Defence on Sunday, he is still ploughing his way through the various documents, but on the basis of my review yesterday evening, at present there are 33 documents which are not yet exhibited. I'm leaving out all the ones on our list which are already exhibits which he can speak to. And therefore, I would wish to call him to deal with those documents. That -- working on a rough average of ten minutes per document, 33 documents, give or take, is something in the region of between three and four hours. Therefore, my application is that I may have four hours with him on top of his 92 ter package. Your Honours, can I say he's the last witness, really, who apart from being part and parcel for a time of the police, then the Ministry of Justice, and has intimate knowledge of Mr. Stanisic and other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership, that I would ask for that amount of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Five hours?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Four hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Four hours --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We originally asked for six and I'm reducing it to four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Four plus the half hour or the 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I suppose it takes -- it takes 20 minutes just to establish that they've said all this before. Four hours -- I would say four hours in total, give or take.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, my maths is terrible. That would be 5.5 hours, but, Your Honour, I would hope to do it in 4. I'm told that my maths on 33 documents, 10 minutes each, works out to 5.5, not 4. But one way or another, I will just have to try and keep it under 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mrs. Korner, I'm a bit lost here. I'm unsure about whether you're asking for four hours, four and a half hours, or five hours, or still six hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not asking -- I'm not asking -- well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: All inclusive.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I have an all-inclusive six hours in the hopes that I can do it in a lot less?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, one of the documents I know for sure is a video that we're going to play, so that always takes a little bit more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the -- you would be permitted six hours with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: All inclusive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That's a total of six hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour, I think we need to go into closed session --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we redact? Yes, Your Honours, can we -- can we go into private session, then closed, and Mr. Olmsted will deal with that. And, Your Honours, would Your Honours then excuse me once Mr. Olmsted has made his application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.
